content: Patients were treated with various regimens of direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) for chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection. Specifically, 126 patients received a combination of sofosbuvir (SOF) and daclatasvir (DCV) for 12 weeks, while two patients were treated with the same regimen for 24 weeks. Another group of 102 patients underwent treatment with sofosbuvir and velpatasvir (SOF + VEL) for 12 weeks. Additionally, 47 patients were treated with glecaprevir and pibrentasvir (GLC + PIB) for varying durations: 44 patients for 8 weeks and 3 patients (with genotype 3 and prior treatment experience) for 16 weeks. Among these, only five patients with cirrhosis were included, all of whom were treated with the SOF + DCV regimen. In the SOF + DCV group, 14 adolescents had genotype 3 HCV, and one had prior treatment experience. In the GLC + PIB group, 22 patients had prior treatment experience. Studies investigating other regimens reported the lowest sustained virologic response at 12 weeks (SVR12) in one group treated with SOF + ribavirin (RBV), with a success rate of only 5%. Details of treatment discontinuations are provided in the referenced studies. A meta-analysis of adolescents aged 12–18 years with chronic HCV infection treated with DAAs showed high rates of SVR12. Regimens included SOF + DCV, SOF + VEL, and GLC + PIB. The analysis also considered factors such as treatment duration, use of RBV, cirrhosis status, genotype, and prior treatment experience. For example, in the SOF + DCV group, 113 out of 126 patients achieved SVR12 after 12 weeks of treatment, while 2 out of 2 patients achieved SVR12 after 24 weeks. In the SOF + VEL group, all 102 patients achieved SVR12 after 12 weeks. In the GLC + PIB group, 48 out of 48 patients achieved SVR12 after 8 weeks of treatment. Adverse events were reported across different age groups. Among children aged 3–5 years, 72% experienced at least one adverse event, with vomiting (21%), cough (14%), and diarrhea (9%) being the most common. A serious adverse event involving accidental ribavirin overdose occurred in a three-year-old patient, requiring hospitalization, but the patient completed treatment and achieved SVR12. In children aged 6–11 years, 53% experienced adverse events, with headache (22%), fatigue (16%), and abdominal pain (10%) being the most frequent. A nine-year-old boy treated with ombitasvir (OBV), paritaprevir (PTV), ritonavir, and other drugs experienced respiratory illness-related events. In adolescents aged 12–18 years, 50% reported adverse events, with headache (22%), fatigue (14%), and nausea (9%) being the most common. Serious adverse events included pneumonia, fractures, and hypotension, though these were not always drug-related. The quality of life (QoL) of children with HCV infection was significantly impacted. Studies showed that HCV infection negatively affected physical, psychosocial, and cognitive functioning, as well as family dynamics. Caregivers reported higher stress levels and concerns about their children’s health and behavior. Despite these challenges, DAA treatment improved QoL in some cases. For example, adolescents treated with SOF + ledipasvir (LDV) achieved a 97% SVR12 rate, and caregivers reported significant improvements in emotional and school functioning scores post-treatment. However, self-reported QoL scores among adolescents remained unchanged at baseline and post-treatment. In summary, DAAs are highly effective in achieving SVR12 in adolescents and children with chronic HCV infection, with minimal serious adverse events. However, the infection and its treatment can significantly impact QoL, highlighting the importance of comprehensive care and support for affected children and their families.
